episodes.episode_title: How Do I Define My New Role to Set Myself Up for Success?
episodes.guest: an operations leader coached by Muriel Wilkins, identified only as Jules to protect her confidentiality
episodes.listening_range: The full episode is one coaching session and runs long, roughly 60 minutes. This file holds the assigned section, about 45 minutes: the coaching from the point where they turn to the concern about not being technical enough, through the boundary-setting near the end. The publisher transcript carries no timecodes, so these figures are estimated from speech rate; use the spoken start and end lines as the markers.
episodes.the_idea: Jules has led teams for years and now gets to design her own next role. The part that matters for this course is buried in the middle. In her first leadership job a colleague set out to push her out, told her team and her peers she was not qualified and that he should have her job, and kept it up for months. She did the by-the-book thing, went to HR and her manager, and nobody acted for a long time. He was finally removed, but her confidence was, in her words, completely shot. What she does with that is the lesson. She names what she would do next time, go big and document and make noise, and her coach presses on two quieter moves: not letting the other person's voice become her own, and building the kind of confidence that comes from knowing she can handle whatever happens rather than from things going her way. Then she sets concrete boundaries with a boss who says the right things but may not act on them. It is the course with the polish taken off, because the official channels failed her.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: The episode is framed as designing a new role, but the part that matters here is the hostile stretch inside it and what she does with it. Three things. First, the story from her first leadership role: a colleague who had it out for her, told others she was not qualified and that he should have her job, and kept it up for months; what she did, which was go to HR and her manager, and how they responded, which was that nobody was bold enough to act for a long time and her confidence was completely shot. Second, what she says she would do if attacked again, meaning fight, go big, document everything, go to HR, make a lot of noise, and her coach's two cautions: do not let someone else's voice become your voice, and confidence comes from knowing you can deal with whatever happens. Third, the boundary-setting near the end with a manager who says the right things but may not back them. Skip the vacation and house-buying analogies and the general career-design talk.

questions.question: In her first leadership role, what did the colleague who had it out for her actually do, what did she do about it, and how did HR and her manager respond?

Muriel warns against letting someone else's voice become your voice. Name one message about yourself that your own resistant environment has half-convinced you of, and one concrete way you would test whether it is true.

Jules says that next time she would go big, document everything, and go to HR. The first time, those channels were slow and nobody was bold enough to act. Where would the official channels fail you the same way, and what would you do instead?

episodes.episode_title: Episode 42: Biolore: India's most aggressive botanical invaders
episodes.guest: invasion biologists Ankila Hiremath, Manzoor Shah and Ninad Mungi, with host Subhra Priyadarshini
episodes.listening_range: Approximately 00:07 to 26:11, about 26 minutes of the roughly 30 minute episode. The transcript is timestamped, so use those markers. The file holds only this section; the sponsor announcements at 00:01 and 29:34 are left out.
episodes.the_idea: Ecology gives the course a lens with no villain in it. A plant that behaves at home turns invasive somewhere else only when two things line up: it spreads and it does harm. What lets it run is not malice, it is conditions. An opened forest canopy, the rubble of a bombed city, the missing pests and grazers that held it in check back home. The read for a change effort is direct. Entrenched resistance and toxic behavior spread when the system is disturbed and the usual checks are gone, not because one person is evil. The hard part matches too. Pull one invasive plant and walk away and it is back in three or four years, so removal without restoration fails, the way removing one bad actor rarely fixes a culture. And the scientists close on a warning the course needs: sometimes the invader becomes load-bearing, holding a working novel ecosystem together, so not everything you have labeled resistance should be ripped out.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: The transcript is timestamped, so go straight to it. Three things. First, how the scientists separate an invasive species from one that is only alien or naturalized, at about 03:04, and the conditions that let an introduced plant explode in a new place: disturbance, missing natural enemies and genetic mixing. The Conyza canadensis story from about 12:42 to 15:59 is the clearest case, including how the World War Two bombing of London opened ground for invaders. Second, why removal on its own does not work and why prevention matters, about 16:23 to 17:07: the line that a late invasion is like cancer in its last stage, and that Lantana grows back in three or four years unless removal is followed by restoration. Third, the twist from about 23:21 to 26:11 that the same plant behaves differently by context and can settle into a working novel ecosystem. Skip the colonial history of how Lantana reached India and the genomics detail.

questions.question: The scientists separate an invasive species from one that is merely alien or naturalized. What two things must be true for something to count as invasive, and name one condition they say lets an introduced species take off in a new place?

Ankila says removing Lantana without restoration just brings it back in three or four years. In your own change effort, name one harmful behavior you could remove that would simply grow back, and what restoration would have to follow the removal.

Ninad describes an invasive plant that became part of a working novel ecosystem that supports local life. Where in your organization might something you have labeled resistance or toxicity be holding something valuable together, and how would you tell the difference?

episodes.episode_title: Dr. Bayo Akomolafe on Slowing Down in Urgent Times /155
episodes.guest: Bayo Akomolafe, Nigerian philosopher and author, with host Ayana Young
episodes.listening_range: One stretch from the second half of the roughly 55 minute episode, about 20 minutes of listening. The For The Wild transcript carries no timecodes, so the timing is estimated from speech rate; use the spoken start and end lines as the real markers.
episodes.the_idea: This course runs on action. Name the toxic or resistant system, set boundaries, build resilience, reclaim your power, leave if you must. Akomolafe, a Nigerian philosopher, argues that the reflex itself can be part of the problem. His line is that in trying to escape the prison, the prison gains its form, and that in pursuing justice on the system's own terms we reinforce the thing we are trying to leave. He splits power as dominion and control, which is the kind you try to reclaim, from what he calls other spaces of power, which he reaches through a Yoruba story about the trickster Eshu. He lands on a question that unsettles the whole course: what if the way to respond to crisis is part of the crisis? It is a real argument against the course default, not a tactic that sits inside it.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: This one argues against the course. Three things to hold on to in the assigned stretch. First, his claim that fighting a system on its own terms can feed it: in pursuing justice we reinforce the system we are trying to escape, and in trying to escape the prison, the prison gains its form. Second, his split between power as dominion and control, the kind you try to reclaim, and what he calls other spaces of power, which he reaches through the Yoruba Eshu story and the line that the world exceeds our notions of power and justice. Third, the post-activism question he lands on, what if the way to respond to crisis is part of the crisis, set next to Ayana's own pull between a duty to fight and sitting with the trouble. Skip the earlier climate and Anthropocene framing and the later talk on failure and allyship.

questions.question: Akomolafe says fighting a system on its own terms can backfire. Complete his image: in trying to escape the prison, the prison does what? And say what he means by his post-activism question about how we respond to crisis.

He separates power as dominion from what he calls other spaces of power. In your resistant environment, name one move you make to reclaim power that actually runs on the system's own logic, and what a different kind of power might look like.

The course tells you to name toxicity and act on it, set boundaries, reclaim power, and leave if needed. Akomolafe suggests that reflex can be part of the crisis. Where might he be right about your situation, and where do you think he is simply wrong for a workplace?
